"A rattling noise started on cold starts. Lasted about two seconds, then stopped. The oil level was fine. I thought it was just a diesel sound - except my car isn't a diesel. A friend said, 'That's the death rattle. Don't drive it. Get it towed.' I listened. Best decision I ever made." A mechanically minded friend recognised it as the "death rattle" and advised towing the car rather than driving. Model Audi A4 B8 Year 2010 Engine 2.0 TFSI (CAEB) - EA888 Gen2 First symptom 85,000 miles Repair mileage 87,000 miles Service history Full Audi main dealer history Disclaimer: This is a representative scenario based on common failure patterns observed across VW/Audi EA888 Gen3 (n=130) diesel and petrol variant quote requests on Engines Market in 2025 [ESTIMATED - using EA888 Gen3 data as proxy for CAEB platform], combined with workshop consensus. Individual outcomes vary. The death rattle The sound that told the owner to stop driving immediately. The owner first noticed a brief rattling noise on cold starts around 85,000 miles. The noise lasted approximately two seconds after ignition, then disappeared. The car drove normally otherwise - no loss of power, no warning lights. What they thought "Maybe it's just the engine settling." Oil level was fine. No warning lights. Car drove normally. What it actually was Spring-loaded tensioner failing The original design can fail without warning. When it fails, the chain jumps and pistons collide with valves. The intervention Friend recognised it "That's the death rattle. Don't drive it. Get it towed." The owner listened. The 2.0 TFSI (EA888 Gen2) is equipped with a timing chain tensioner that uses a spring-loaded design rather than oil pressure alone. According to workshop consensus [INDUSTRY ESTIMATE], the original tensioner design can fail without warning. Timeline From death rattle to preventative repair - caught just in time. The owner mentioned the noise to a mechanically minded friend, who immediately recognised it as the "death rattle" - the sound of a failing timing chain tensioner. The friend advised towing the vehicle to a specialist rather than driving. What the owner noticed A brief cold-start rattle became more noticeable over 2,000 miles. What was happening internally The tensioner piston was extending beyond spec. The chain had stretched. Failure was imminent. Workshop diagnosis The specialist found the tensioner on borrowed time. The specialist removed the timing cover inspection port and performed a borescope inspection. The findings confirmed the owner had caught the failure just in time. Timing chain tensioner Original spring-loaded design - known failure risk Timing chain Stretched - measured beyond service limit Chain guides Visible wear - tensioner piston extended beyond spec Camshaft timing Within specification - no jump detected (caught early) Valves No contact with pistons (failure avoided) Oil pressure Normal Specialist summary "The tensioner hasn't failed yet, but it's on borrowed time. The chain has stretched, and the tensioner is nearly at its maximum extension. If you keep driving, the chain will eventually jump time. When that happens, the pistons hit the valves. That's a £5,000 engine replacement. We can replace the chain, guides, and updated tensioner now for £1,800." Repair options Three choices: wait for failure, replace properly, or go new engine.
